content: Caffeine citrate, administered orally, is a methylxanthine compound approved by the FDA for the treatment of apnea of prematurity in infants born between 28 and less than 33 weeks of gestational age. Common side effects include irritability and feeding difficulties. Adult Indications and Dosage There is limited information available regarding the FDA-approved or off-label use of oral caffeine citrate in adult patients. Pediatric Indications and Dosage Caffeine citrate, available as an injection or oral solution, is indicated for the short-term treatment of apnea of prematurity in infants between 28 and less than 33 weeks of gestational age. Before initiating treatment, baseline serum caffeine levels should be measured in infants previously treated with theophylline, as preterm infants metabolize theophylline into caffeine. Similarly, baseline caffeine levels should be assessed in infants born to mothers who consumed caffeine during pregnancy, as caffeine readily crosses the placenta. The recommended loading dose and maintenance doses of caffeine citrate are provided in the drug label. It is important to note that 20 mg of caffeine citrate is equivalent to 10 mg of caffeine base. Serum caffeine concentrations should be monitored periodically during treatment to avoid toxicity, as serious toxicity has been associated with serum levels exceeding 50 mg/L. The solution should be visually inspected for particulate matter or discoloration before administration, and any vials with discolored or particulate-containing solutions should be discarded. Contraindications Caffeine citrate is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to any of its components. Warnings During a double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, six cases of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) were reported among 85 infants studied (46 in the caffeine group and 39 in the placebo group). Three of these cases resulted in death, and five of the six NEC cases occurred in infants exposed to caffeine citrate. Although a causal relationship between methylxanthine use and NEC has not been established, patients treated with caffeine citrate should be closely monitored for the development of NEC. Adverse Reactions In clinical trials, the overall number of adverse events reported during the double-blind period was similar between the caffeine citrate and placebo groups. However, adverse events more frequently observed in caffeine-treated patients included central nervous system stimulation (e.g., irritability, restlessness, jitteriness), cardiovascular effects (e.g., tachycardia, increased left ventricular output, increased stroke volume), gastrointestinal effects (e.g., increased gastric aspirate, gastrointestinal intolerance), alterations in serum glucose (e.g., hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia), and renal effects (e.g., increased urine flow rate, increased creatinine clearance, increased sodium and calcium excretion). Long-term follow-up studies have not shown caffeine to adversely affect neurological development or growth parameters. Drug Interactions Caffeine is primarily metabolized by the cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) enzyme, and it has the potential to interact with drugs that are substrates, inhibitors, or inducers of CYP1A2. Limited data exist on drug interactions with caffeine in preterm neonates. Concurrent administration of caffeine with ketoprofen has been shown to reduce urine volume in healthy volunteers, but the clinical significance of this interaction in preterm neonates is unknown. Interconversion between caffeine and theophylline has been reported in preterm neonates, and concurrent use of these drugs is not recommended. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Caffeine citrate is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. While teratogenicity concerns are not relevant when administered to infants, studies in pregnant animals have shown a low incidence of fetal malformations (e.g., cleft palate, exencephaly) at high doses. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Labor and Delivery: There is no FDA guidance on the use of caffeine citrate during labor and delivery. Nursing Mothers: There is no FDA guidance on the use of caffeine citrate in nursing mothers. Pediatric Use: Caffeine citrate is specifically indicated for use in preterm neonates with apnea of prematurity. Geriatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of caffeine citrate in geriatric patients. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: Caffeine citrate should be used with caution in preterm neonates with impaired renal or hepatic function. Serum caffeine concentrations should be monitored, and dosage adjustments should be made to avoid toxicity. Administration and Monitoring Caffeine citrate is administered orally or intravenously. Serum caffeine levels should be monitored periodically to ensure therapeutic efficacy and avoid toxicity. Overdosage Limited information is available regarding caffeine citrate overdose. In cases of suspected overdose, contact the National Poison Help hotline immediately. Pharmacology Caffeine is structurally related to other methylxanthines, such as theophylline and theobromine. It acts as a bronchial smooth muscle relaxant, central nervous system stimulant, cardiac muscle stimulant, and diuretic. The exact mechanism of action in apnea of prematurity is not fully understood but is hypothesized to involve stimulation of the respiratory center, increased minute ventilation, decreased threshold to hypercapnia, increased response to hypercapnia, increased skeletal muscle tone, decreased diaphragmatic fatigue, increased metabolic rate, and increased oxygen consumption. These effects are primarily attributed to caffeine's antagonism of adenosine receptors. Pharmacokinetics Absorption: After oral administration of 10 mg caffeine base/kg to preterm neonates, peak plasma levels (Cmax) range from 6-10 mg/L, with a mean time to peak concentration (Tmax) of 30 minutes to 2 hours. Tmax is not affected by formula feeding. Distribution: Caffeine is rapidly distributed into the brain, and cerebrospinal fluid levels approximate plasma levels. Plasma protein binding in neonates is not well-documented. Metabolism: Caffeine metabolism in preterm neonates is limited due to immature hepatic enzyme systems. Interconversion between caffeine and theophylline has been reported. Elimination: Caffeine elimination is slower in neonates compared to adults due to immature hepatic and renal function. The mean half-life (T1/2) in neonates is approximately 3-4 days, and 86% of caffeine is excreted unchanged in urine within 6 days. By 9 months of age, caffeine metabolism approximates that of adults (T1/2 = 5 hours, 1% excreted unchanged). Clinical Studies A multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial compared caffeine citrate to placebo in 85 preterm infants with apnea of prematurity. The study demonstrated a significantly greater percentage of apnea-free patients on day 2 of treatment in the caffeine group compared to the placebo group. How Supplied Caffeine citrate is available as a clear, colorless, sterile, preservative-free aqueous solution in 3 mL glass vials. Each vial contains 20 mg/mL caffeine citrate (equivalent to 10 mg/mL caffeine base). The solution should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F).
